reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes cloud mining for passive income, provides a registration referral, and directs viewers to purchase hashrate to start earning. It presents prior profit and projected figures alongside a stated withdrawal-fee increase; the available video evidence does not establish actual payouts or losses, and does not establish that the separate ICO bonus was connected to the mining offer.

citations.quote: Want passive income? Then this is for you. https://hashflare.io/r/DB9A1A1C - registration.
buy a hashrate, select one of the points and buy on the minimum amount $20 worth dollars
you will also register and start earning on him
the most profitable is this f2 pool
before i had profit of $1.76 today I changed setting

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker does not present mining as something a newcomer should enter blindly. He tells viewers unfamiliar with cloud mining to learn what it is first, acknowledges increased withdrawal fees, and describes the cryptocurrency rate as unstable. His pool recommendation is expressly tied to the current date, and he says he will observe how a settings change affects revenue later. Those qualifications matter: the cited earnings figure is a report of his prior experience, not a demonstrated promise that viewers will receive the same return.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites a registration link, a purchase instruction, and reported profit, but those do not establish a guaranteed return or concealment of costs. The speaker also discusses an increased withdrawal commission and says he must wait to see how the pool change affects revenue. Read together, the statements are a qualified account of a mining choice, even though the speaker recommends the service.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Advising beginners to read up and mentioning fees do not undo the solicitation. The description pitches passive income through a registration link, while the speaker tells viewers to buy hashrate and says they can register and start earning. His uncertainty about a pool adjustment does not qualify that broader earning pitch.

opening.argument: Judge, the title asks which SHA-256 pool to choose, and the speaker spends time explaining his pool settings, the three-pool limit he encountered, and the change he made that day. He also walks through the Reinvest function. The sampled dashboard view shows SHA-256 capacity and pool-related charts. That makes the earnings figure relevant as an observation in a settings demonstration, not proof of a promised payout. The registration link is present, but it should be weighed against what the presentation actually spends time demonstrating.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the referral and purchase passage as defining the entire video. Yet the title poses a pool-selection question, and the speaker describes changing pools to observe what happens to revenue. The quoted $1.76 is a before-change figure, not a forecast that a viewer buying hashrate will earn $1.76. The instruction is real, but it appears within a demonstration of account settings.

citations.quote: Which pool is better to choose in HashFlare on SHA-256?
before i had profit of $1.76 today I changed setting and we will see how change this revenue

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A settings demonstration can still promote a paid earning scheme. Here, the description invites viewers seeking passive income to register; the speaker supplies a minimum purchase amount and says registration leads to earning. Pool controls explain how the product works, but they do not remove the invitation to buy mining capacity for returns.

citations.quote: Want passive income? Then this is for you. https://hashflare.io/r/DB9A1A1C - registration.

opening.argument: Judge, the visible transaction being discussed is the purchase of mining capacity: the speaker gives a minimum price, discusses the price of capacity, and compares mining options. The sampled account screen displays a SHA-256 section with capacity and charts. A registration referral is disclosed in the description. Those facts can describe promotion of a paid service; they do not, by themselves, show a guaranteed return, a request for viewers' credentials, or a completed withdrawal that was refused. The record supports scrutiny of the earning pitch, but not an inference that every advertised mining purchase shown here is deceptive.

Its own account concedes that actual payouts or losses are not established. The speaker's discussion of buying capacity and selecting a pool can therefore be read as explaining a priced mining service, without treating its claims as verified.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The issue is the mechanism promoted, not proof that a particular withdrawal failed. The description offers passive income through registration, and the speaker connects buying hashrate with registering and earning. Calling capacity a priced service does not change the paid-mining-return proposition presented to viewers; the dashboard view does not verify that viewers will receive those returns.
